title: At 60, can we still buy property to live off the rent?
excerpt: A couple in their 60s with RM450,000 in EPF and a flat that barely appreciated hope a rental unit can fund their retirement. Sean explains why that is hard now, and what he would do first.

qa.asker: A viewer in her 60s who wrote in by email
qa.context: She is 60 and her husband, 63, a company driver earning about RM4,300 with overtime, wants to stop working. They have about RM450,000 in EPF and no insurance. Their own flat off Old Klang Road, bought 22 years ago for RM166,000, sells for about RM270,000 and would rent for about RM1,000, though tenants there often pay late or leave. They need about RM3,000 a month to live, also want a separate place for an adult son who needs his own space, and a relative has offered RM2,500 a month for four years.
qa.question: Is it too late to buy a property that generates rental income, how could they get a loan at 63, and should they sell or rent out their flat?
qa.quote: Take control of your life instead of hoping for things to happen.
qa.answer: Keep their flat as the family home and safety net. At their age, a unit whose rent exceeds its instalment by RM1,000 or more is rare, perhaps 3% to 5% of properties, and hard to finance. Focus first on active income, like part-time agency or customer service work. Learn how property investing works before committing their EPF.

reasons.title: Late loans are hard to get
reasons.body: Banks lend to about age 70, so at 63 a loan is very difficult. Their younger son could apply once he has worked six months to a year, with a parent supporting the application.

reasons.title: Retail buyers pay the highest price
reasons.body: Developers sell the best units to staff, relatives and associates first, so the public pays the most. A unit that pays out more than its instalment usually needs a below-market price and active management, such as renting room by room.

reasons.title: Their flat did appreciate
reasons.body: Rising from RM166,000 to about RM270,000 is a gain of more than 50%, even if it felt slow. Selling it would leave them needing somewhere else to live.

reasons.title: Tenants can be managed
reasons.body: Screening where tenants work and how many will live there, offering one-year leases and furnishing the unit well all reduce late payments and damage.

actions: Keep the current flat as their home and last resort.
Look for active income both can do, such as property agency, customer service from home, or sharing their experience online.
Learn about property investing before spending any EPF savings on it.
Plan any future loan around their younger son's income once he is working.
Look after their health, since they have no insurance.
qa.caveat: Sean can't give a precise plan for their family situation, which involves care decisions only they can make. His point is that rental income is a slow tool, best started young, and not a quick fix at 60.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #188. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in September 2022, and family details are kept to what the answer needs. Sean says he is a client of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase company, and suggests learning from it.
